title: Can't Pay Your Bills? A Calm Step-by-Step Triage Guide
description: Can't pay your bills this month? A calm triage guide: what to pay first, what happens if a bill is late, call scripts and where to find help.

cover.alt: A stack of envelopes, a phone and a cup of tea on a wooden table

keywords: cant pay my bills what bills to pay first behind on bills hardship plan late rent utility shutoff
takeaways: Write every bill down, then pay in order: housing, utilities, food, transport to work, then debt minimums.
Call before the due date. Most landlords and companies have more options for people who ask early.
Download the free bill triage worksheet to see which bills your money covers and which need a call.
body:
If you have typed "can't pay my bills what to do" into a search bar at 2 a.m., take a breath. One bad month is not a broken life, and it does not mean you are bad with money. Hours get cut. Cars break. Rent goes up. What matters now is paying the right things first, calling the right people early, and knowing which deadlines are real and which are just alarming words on an envelope. This guide is a triage plan. You will sort your bills by what they protect, see what actually happens if each one runs late, use short phone scripts to ask for more time, and find real programs built for exactly this situation. No shame, no scare tactics, no empty promises. ## Step 1: Get every bill out of your head and onto paper Worry grows in the dark. A list shrinks it. Write down every bill you owe this month: the name, the amount, the due date, and whether it is already late. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) puts this first in its guidance for people who fall behind, because you cannot make calm choices about bills you have not fully listed. Add up the total, then write down the money you actually have and what is still coming in this month. The gap between those numbers is your real problem, and it is usually smaller and more specific than the dread you have been carrying around. A specific gap can be worked on. A vague one just sits on your chest. If a spreadsheet helps you think, we made a free one for this exact job, with a row for each bill, its due date, and the order to pay it in.

Download the free Bill Triage Worksheet (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The bill triage worksheet listing bills by priority, with a plan column showing which to pay and which need a call first](/assets/img/posts/bill-triage-worksheet-preview-1180x706.webp) Once the list exists, the rest gets easier. If money is tight most months, not just this one, a simple plan built for a small income helps too. Read next: [How to Make a Budget When You Earn Less Than $1,000 a Month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/). ## Step 2: Pay in this order, and know why When there is not enough for everything, the order you pay in matters more than the amounts. Pay first for the things that keep you housed, warm, fed, and able to earn. Everything else comes after that. Collection calls are uncomfortable. Losing your home or your job is worse, so do not let the loudest bill jump the queue. | Order | Bill | Why it sits here | |-------|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | 1 | Rent or mortgage | A roof keeps every other part of life possible, and housing cases move faster than most debts. | | 2 | Utilities: electric, gas, water, heat | A home without power or water is barely a home, and reconnection fees add costs you do not need. | | 3 | Food | Keep it basic this month. You cannot earn or think straight while hungry. | | 4 | Transport to work, plus car insurance | Your income is the way out of this. Protect the bus pass, the fuel, and the insurance that keeps you legal. | | 5 | Minimum payments on cards and loans | Minimums keep accounts in good standing once the basics above are safe. | | 6 | Everything else | Subscriptions, gym, extras. Pause or cancel them today. They can come back later. | Here is that order at work. This is an illustration with made-up numbers, not a real person's story. Jordan has $1,260 for bills this month and owes $1,344, so something has to wait. Rent is $900, the electric bill is $95, a basic grocery shop is $180, and fuel to get to work is $75. Those four add up to $1,250, which leaves $10. The $45 phone bill, the $35 card minimum, and a $14 streaming plan cannot all be paid, so Jordan cancels the streaming plan, calls the card company about the minimum (script below), and asks the phone company to move the due date. The home stays warm, the job stays reachable, and every company involved hears from Jordan before a deadline passes, which is what gives them room to say yes. ## Step 3: What actually happens if a bill is late Fear fills in the blanks with the worst version. The real timelines are slower than most people fear, and slow means you have time to act. Rules vary by state, company, and contract, so treat this as a general map, not a promise about your exact case. | Bill | First days late | As weeks pass | |--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Rent | A late fee may be added after any grace period in your lease. | The landlord can start the formal eviction process, which runs through the courts. Nobody can legally lock you out without a court order in the US, and the process takes time. | | Utilities | The balance rolls forward. You may get a reminder notice. | After notice, shutoff becomes possible once a bill is well past due. Many states limit shutoffs in extreme weather, and most companies offer payment plans if you ask before the shutoff date. | | Credit card | A late fee can be charged right away, plus interest. | Issuers generally do not report a missed payment to the credit bureaus until it is 30 days past due. Paying inside that window can protect your credit record. | | Car loan | A late fee may apply after the grace period in your contract. | The lender can treat the loan as in default, and repossession becomes a real risk over time, which is why this call matters early. | | Phone and internet | A late fee, then slower service or suspension. | Service can be cut and the balance sent to collections, but no home or job is at stake. That is why these bills sit lower on the list. | Read the pattern in that table. Almost nothing terrible happens on day one. Almost everything gets worse when a company hears nothing from you for a month. Silence turns a late bill into a legal problem, so the next step protects you most. ## Step 4: Make the calls, using these scripts The CFPB's advice for anyone falling behind is simple: call your creditors before you miss the payment, explain plainly, and ask what they can do. Companies have hardship options they rarely advertise, because most people never ask. You do not need to be a smooth talker. Be early, honest, and specific about what you can pay and when. Before you dial, have your account number, the amount you can pay today, and the date you can pay the rest. Write down the name of the person you spoke to and what was agreed. If it is not written down, it is hard to prove later. ### Calling your landlord *"Hi, this is [your name] at [your address]. I am calling before rent is due, not after. My hours were cut this month, so I am short. I can pay [amount] on the first and the rest by [date]. Can we agree to that, and can I get it in writing so we both have it?"* Most landlords prefer a plan and a tenant who calls over a vacancy and a court date. If yours agrees, a short email or signed note is enough. These ideas also help when a lease comes up for renewal. Read next: [How to Negotiate Rent](/blog/negotiate-your-rent/). ### Calling a utility company *"Hi, I am calling about account [number]. I cannot pay the full balance this month, and I do not want the account to fall further behind. Do you have a payment plan, a due date extension, or a hardship program? I can pay [amount] today and spread the rest over the next few bills."* Ask also about energy assistance. Many companies will flag your account and hold off on shutoff while an application is processed. Cutting future bills helps the plan stick, too. Read next: [How to Lower Your Electric Bill](/blog/lower-your-electric-bill/). ### Calling a card company or lender *"Hi, I am calling about my account ending in [last digits]. This month is short because [one honest reason]. Can you waive the late fee and set up a hardship plan or a reduced payment for one or two months? Before I agree, can you tell me how it will be reported to the credit bureaus?"* That last question matters. Some hardship plans are reported as paid as agreed, and some are not, and you deserve to know before you say yes. If debt payments stay hard after this month, a full payoff plan is the next job. Read next: [How to Pay Off Credit Card Debt Fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/). ## Step 5: Ask for the help that already exists These programs exist because bad months are common, not because anyone failed. Using them is the system working as intended. - Dial 211 (US). This free, confidential helpline connects you with local help for rent, utility bills, and food. According to 211.org, the network made over 19 million referrals in 2025, including 9.1 million for housing, homelessness, and utility bills. Call 2-1-1 or search 211.org. Canada has a 211 service too. - LIHEAP (US). The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program is a federal program, run through states, that helps households pay heating and cooling bills in every state. Apply through your state or local agency, and ask your utility to note your account while you apply. - Your utility and landlord, again. Many utility companies run their own assistance funds, and many cities and charities run small rent funds that never get advertised. The person on the phone often knows about both. - Food help. A food pantry visit this month can free up real cash for rent. There is no queue of deserving and undeserving people. There is just food, and a month where you need it. Outside the US, the names differ but the shape is the same. In the UK, Citizens Advice and StepChange give free debt help, and energy suppliers must offer payment plans if you ask. In Australia, the National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007) offers free financial counselling, and the government's MoneySmart site covers problems paying bills. Everywhere, the first move is the same: contact the company early and ask what help exists. ## Your first 48 hours: a checklist When money runs short, speed and order protect you more than panic does. Do these in order. 1. Write down every bill due in the next 30 days: who, how much and the due date. 2. Mark the essentials first: rent or mortgage, utilities, food, and getting to work. 3. Check your balance and work out exactly what you can pay this week, not what you wish you could pay. 4. Call the highest-risk creditor first, usually your landlord, before the due date passes. 5. On every call, write down the person's name, the date and time, what was agreed and any reference number. 6. Ask each company about hardship plans, payment breaks or spreading the amount, and get the answer in writing. 7. Pay something toward the essentials rather than clearing one small bill in full and missing rent. 8. Cancel or pause non-essential subscriptions the same day, not next week. 9. Never ignore a letter from a court or a lawyer. It always needs a reply. 10. Do not take a new high-cost loan to pay an old bill without free advice first. 11. Put every new payment date you agreed in your calendar before you finish for the day. ## Two things to skip while you sort this out First, skip payday loans and any quick cash offer with fees you do not fully understand. Borrowing at very high cost to pay a bill usually turns one bad month into three. Second, be wary of companies that charge upfront fees to settle or fix your debts. The CFPB warns people to be skeptical of debt settlement companies for exactly this reason, and free help through nonprofit credit counsellors exists instead. ## When it is more than one bad month Triage is for a rough patch. If the gap is there every month even after you cut back and make the calls, that is not a willpower problem. It is a maths problem, and maths problems have outside help. A nonprofit credit counsellor can review the whole picture with you and contact lenders for you. Asking early gives you more options, not fewer. And when the month turns a corner, even a tiny restart matters. Read next: [How to Build an Emergency Fund on a Low Income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/). ## Frequently asked questions ### Should I pay my credit card or my electric bill first? The electric bill. A card company can charge a fee and wait. Your home needs power and water to stay livable. Pay the utility, then call the card company before the due date and use the script above. ### Will one late payment wreck my credit score? Not on its own, and not right away. Card issuers generally do not report a missed payment until it is 30 days past due, so paying within that window can keep it off your record, though a late fee may still apply. If it is reported, the effect fades over time. ### Can my landlord make me leave straight away for late rent? No. In the US, eviction runs through the courts, and a landlord cannot legally change the locks or remove your things without a court order. Do not ignore any formal notice, though. Read it, note the dates, and get free local advice if one arrives. ### Is 211 really free, and what does it actually do? Yes. Calling 2-1-1 is free and confidential. It is a referral service rather than a fund, so it does not hand you money. It connects you to the rent funds, utility programs, food support, and charities near you, saving you days of searching. ### What if I cannot pay anything at all this month? Call anyway. A company that hears "I can pay nothing this month, here is why, and here is when I will call back" treats you very differently from one that hears silence. Call 211, use food support so your cash can go to housing, and keep every small promise you make. Small kept promises rebuild trust with lenders and with yourself. Disclaimer: This article is general information for education, not financial, legal, or tax advice. Rules on eviction, utility shutoffs, and assistance programs vary by state and country, and they change. For advice on your own case, talk to a nonprofit credit counsellor or a legal aid service. ## Sources - [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, "Behind on bills: Three steps to help you make tough choices in tight moments"](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/behind-bills-three-steps-help-you-make-tough-choices-tight-moments/) - [211, United Way](https://211.org/) - [LIHEAP Clearinghouse, US Department of Health and Human Services, Administration for Children and Families, "Who We Are"](https://liheapch.acf.gov:443/node/1532)
